runs: No strain can promise laughs. Still, the strains that make you laugh tend to share a few traits: a THC-forward profile, bright citrus or sweet aromas and a reputation for upbeat, talkative effects. Just as important are your dose and the people around you. Here's what science suggests about the cannabis giggles, plus classic strains people often link with them and how format changes the experience.

body.text: Why cannabis can turn small things hilarious

runs: You've probably seen it happen. Someone mispronounces a word, and the whole room can't stop laughing for five minutes.

THC changes how you experience the moment. According to NIDA, it can temporarily alter mood, thoughts and perceptions, including your sense of time, and it can make people feel happier or more relaxed. That may be part of why an odd detail can seem hilarious, or a familiar story can feel brand new.

It isn't everyone's experience, though. NIDA also notes that cannabis can leave some people irritable or restless, and that anxiety and panic are more common with large amounts, strong products or little experience. The giggles live in a sweet spot.

body.text: THC, the endocannabinoid system and mood: what's known

runs: Your body runs its own cannabinoid system. The endocannabinoid system is made up of cannabinoid receptors, the body's own cannabinoid compounds, such as anandamide and 2-AG, and the enzymes that make and break them down. CB1 receptors are abundant in the brain and spinal cord.

THC acts on those CB1 receptors, which helps explain its effects on mood and perception. Researchers have learned a great deal about this system, but they haven't found a dedicated laughter switch. No one can predict from a strain name who will laugh and who won't.

body.text: CBD's role, and why it doesn't add laughs on its own

runs: CBD is the other well-known cannabinoid, and NIDA notes that it isn't intoxicating like THC. On its own, it won't bring on the giggles.

Some people assume adding CBD changes how THC feels. A controlled trial published in 2022 tested vaporized cannabis with 10 mg of THC and different amounts of CBD, at ratios common in real products. It found no evidence that CBD changed THC's subjective or pleasurable effects. If laughs are the goal, the THC number and your dose matter far more than the CBD figure.

body.text: Terpenes and laughter: limonene, myrcene and the entourage idea

runs: Terpenes are the aroma compounds that make a strain smell like lemons, pine or fresh earth. Many people believe they shape the high, and research is starting to test that idea, but evidence on laughter itself is thin.

is the bright, citrusy terpene. In mouse studies, citrus oils have shown anti-anxiety-like effects. In a small 2024 study, adults who inhaled limonene along with a high dose of THC reported feeling less anxious and paranoid than with THC alone. THC's other effects didn't change, and limonene by itself did nothing noticeable. The researchers noted that the doses they tested are unlikely in typical retail flower.

If you're hunting for limonene strains, look for terpene data on the label when it's listed, since a lemony name or aroma doesn't promise high levels. The takeaway: early research hints that limonene may take the edge off THC's anxious side, but no study shows that any terpene creates laughter.

Sativa-leaning strains have a reputation for being social and giggly, while indica-leaning ones are known as mellow. Those reputations aren't useless, but they're unreliable, because a strain's label doesn't consistently match its chemistry, as our
explains.
A better approach is to read the label for THC level and terpene notes. If bright, citrusy or sweet strains have made you laugh before, look for similar aromas, whatever the category says.
Notice, too, that most of the classic giggly strains below are hybrids of some kind. That alone shows how blurry the categories have become.

body.text: Laughter is social: set, setting and shared sessions

runs: Here's the part strain lists leave out: laughter is mostly social. Researchers who study it describe laughter as a social emotion, and they note that we are 30 times more likely to laugh with someone else than on our own.
That's why the same strain can feel hilarious at a game night and quiet on a solo evening. A few things help:
Friends who make you laugh sober will likely still be your favorite audience.
A comedy, a card game or a silly playlist gives the giggles somewhere to go.
Familiar, private surroundings help you relax.
Stress or fatigue can tilt the experience the other way.
Enough to lift the mood, not so much that it turns anxious.

items.q: Why does weed make you laugh?

runs: THC changes mood, perception and your sense of time, which can make small things seem funnier than usual. It acts on CB1 receptors in the brain, part of the body's endocannabinoid system. Company matters just as much, since people laugh far more with others than alone. Too much THC can work against you, though, turning giggles into anxiety.

items.q: Which terpene is linked to laughter?

runs: Limonene, the citrus terpene, comes up most often, but no study shows it causes laughter. In a small 2024 lab study, limonene inhaled with a high THC dose lowered ratings of anxiety and paranoia without changing THC's other effects, though the doses were unlikely to come from typical flower. Myrcene has a more relaxing reputation, based largely on animal research. Read terpene notes as clues, not promises.

items.q: Does sativa make you laugh more than indica?

runs: Not reliably. Sativa-leaning strains have a giggly, social reputation, but the label doesn't consistently predict a product's chemistry or how it will feel. THC level, terpenes, your dose and the people around you matter more. If a strain makes you laugh, note its aroma and THC level, and look for similar profiles next time.

items.q: What is the best strain for laughing?

runs: There isn't a single one. Jack Herer, Durban Poison, Super Lemon Haze and Sunset Sherbet often come up, but the same strain can make one person laugh and another simply relax, and batches differ. A moderate dose of a strain you enjoy, shared with people who make you laugh anyway, is a smart way to begin.

items.q: What helps if I get too high?

runs: Stop using cannabis and move somewhere calm. Sip water, have a light snack and breathe slowly; the feeling fades with time. Don't drive. If someone has chest pain, trouble breathing or can't stay awake, call 911. For other questions, Poison Control is available at 1-800-222-1222.
